title: Running through July 12th at the Public #theatre #musicaltheatre #gir...
transcript: I think this new musical is really something special, but you have to know what you're getting into. Girl Interrupted is based on the book of the same name, which was also made into the 1999 film. The musical score is by Aimee Mann, and King Princess is in the cast, by the way, for those who know. And when I say that you should know what you're getting into here, I mean that in three different ways. First of all, you should know that the content is pretty heavy. I'm not familiar with either the book or the movie, so I can't speak to how different it is, but essentially, it's the reflections of a woman who spent time in a psychiatric institution when she was 18 years old, and it can get very dark. Secondly, you should know that despite what the marketing and the press releases say, this is not a “play with music.” It is a musical. The tone of the show is more like what you would see in a play, and the gaps between songs are, like, a few minutes longer than you would normally see in a musical. But by any reasonable definition, it is still a musical. But that brings me to the third thing that you should probably know beforehand, which is that the vibe of the storytelling here is probably not gonna be for everybody. I found it very absorbing in its quiet restraint, but I think some people will Find it hard to connect to. It kinda reminded me of The Band's Visit in that regard. And while it is told chronologically, it's not especially plot driven. It's more like a series of vignettes. The idea being that these are flashes of memory that the narrator is trying to pull together from her blurry, fragmented recollection of this time that she had been trying to forget. Partly to make sense of it for herself, but also to do her best to tell the stories of these women that she knew there, albeit very briefly, and in the process, turning over these stones that reveal the societal issues underneath it all: the way, in which gender bias and lack of understanding of trauma and other thorny issues worm their way in. And in particular, she sort of posits that the line between “normal” and “crazy” is a lot more thin and slippery than we think. I can definitely see how someone would say that the book was a little disjointed or that the character arcs weren't all that fleshed out, but the way it was presented just had me totally locked in. And the characters were portrayed so vividly and honestly by their respective actors, with the help of Jo Bonney’s very grounded, delicate direction. So that was more than enough for me. I actually thought the weaker component was the lyrics, which did tend to skew a little flat and direct, but still, I thought they made it work within the context of this hauntingly beautiful music, especially because the tone WAS more subdued and the songs WERE more spaced out, it ended up giving the relatively simplistic lyrics a more cathartic and incisive quality that might have read as more trite in a show that was more heavily musicalized. And I wanna emphasize again, it also helps that the music is absolutely gorgeous. One of the most beautiful scores of a musical I've heard in a while.
